title: Coping after you've lost a baby | NHS inform
text:
Coping after you’ve lost a baby
Losing a baby can be a very difficult time, no matter how far along you were.
You may have different feelings and emotions. Some people find they’re deeply affected by losing a baby. Others find they feel more removed. You may also find it difficult to work out exactly what you’re feeling and why. These are all normal reactions. It’s also normal to have different feelings day to day. Emotions after a loss can be unpredictable.
After losing a baby, your body will experience changing hormone levels. These will influence your mood. You may feel like crying a lot. Remember to allow for this and be kind to yourself.
If you start to worry about how you’re feeling, contact your GP practice or another support organisation.
Speak to your GP practice if:
You or someone else has symptoms of depression like:
continuous low mood or sadness
lack of motivation
feeling hopeless and helpless
feeling anxious or worried
disturbed sleep
avoiding contact with family and friends
feeling overwhelmed by daily life and the needs of your home, work or family life
Read more about your
mental wellbeing and getting support
.
Things you can do after losing a baby
If you’ve experienced baby loss, there are some things you can do to try to help you cope.
Mark your loss
You may like to find a special way to remember your pregnancy. You could do something that makes you feel like you’ve said goodbye.
Some people choose to create a memory box, or to create a special corner in a garden dedicated to their baby.
There’s no formal registration process for babies born before 24 weeks. However, you can record your loss in the
Memorial Book of Pregnancy and Baby Loss Prior to 24 Weeks
.
For stillbirths (babies born after 24 weeks), you’ll need to make funeral arrangements for your baby.
Read more about what to do after a stillbirth
Talk to people
You can find peer support in many places, including:
online
though volunteer phonelines
through groups on social media
Sometimes it can help to talk to a professional counsellor. This can be done on your own, or with your partner, if you have one. Your GP can refer you to NHS counselling services or you may be able to refer yourself.
Find ways to express how you feel
It’s important to find ways to express how you feel, but this doesn’t always have to be through talking to someone. Some people find that keeping a diary or journal helps them make sense of their feelings.
Talk with your partner if you have one
You may find that your partner is behaving differently than you. This is because they have different feelings about the loss. They’ll also have different ways of coping with the loss. This does not mean your partner is not also grieving the loss of your baby.
Talking with your partner can help you understand how they’re feeling. It can also help you support each other at this difficult time.
Try to get enough sleep
Emotional stress can make you very tired. It can also make it very difficult to sleep, even if you feel exhausted.
Try to maintain good sleep during this time, and let yourself rest when you need to..
Further help for sleep problems
Remember your loss was not your fault
You may feel guilt over losing your baby, and may wonder if you could have done more to prevent the loss. These are irrational thoughts, but they can eat away at you.
It’s important to remember that it’s unlikely that you lost your baby because of something you did or did not do.
Read more about the causes of a miscarriage
Read more about how an ectopic pregnancy happens
Read more about why a molar pregnancy happens
Read more about the causes of a stillbirth
Emotions you may feel after losing a baby
Feeling sad is an understandable part of losing a baby. It’s ok to feel sad and to grieve for your loss, no matter how far along you were. But you may also feel other emotions.
Shock
Losing a baby can come as a huge shock, especially if it was unexpected. You may need time to make sense of what’s happened and to come to terms with it.
Emptiness
Losing a baby can leave you feeling physically and emotionally empty. It’s common to think nothing much matters anymore. Other people’s problems may feel trivial in comparison to yours. This can make it hard to listen to other people.
Powerless
You can’t fully control when you get pregnant or whether you’ll stay pregnant. All you can do is follow advice and prepare your body as best as you can. This can make you feel powerless. You may feel scared that you can’t prevent another loss should you become pregnant again.
You may also feel let down by your body. You may mistrust your body in future pregnancies and resent the fact that you can’t enjoy your pregnancy.
Anxious
You may be afraid and anxious that you could lose another baby in the future. This is a natural reaction, particularly if you don’t know why you lost your baby, or if it’s happened more than once.
These anxieties may get worse if you get pregnant again. It may help to talk to someone about how you feel now. Your GP will be able to help you access the support you need.
You may also sometimes feel more general anxiety. When something awful happens, it’s easier to imagine other things going wrong too.
Read more about anxiety
Jealous
If you know someone else who is pregnant, or who has a young baby, you may find yourself feeling jealous of them. You may resent them, and be unable to be happy for them. You may also feel bad about feeling this way, making you feel worse.
It may help to know that lots of people feel this way after experiencing baby loss. While it’s important not to isolate yourself, sometimes it helps to reduce contact with people who are triggering these feelings. If you have a strong relationship, you may even be able to explain to them how you feel. If they’re people you see on social media channels, it may help to avoid social media for a while.
Lonely or isolated
You may feel alone, especially if you hadn’t yet told people you were pregnant. You may also feel that no one understands what you’re going through.
Think about whether you might want to tell your employer, a close colleague, friends or family. Being able to talk about your loss might help you to feel less lonely and better supported.
Your loss and your mental health
It can be hard to tell the difference between grief and problems with your mental wellbeing. Depression can be particularly hard to recognise when you’re grieving.
People who are grieving find their feelings of sadness and loss come and go. They’re still able to enjoy things and look forward to the future. This is a normal part of the grieving process.
People who are depressed constantly feel sad. They find it difficult to enjoy anything or be positive about the future. The symptoms of depression can last for weeks or months. They can interfere with your work, social life and family life.
Read more about depression
Some people who’ve lost a baby might also experience:
anxiety
post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
perinatal obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)
Read more about your
mental health and getting support
Finding support after your loss
If you’re struggling to cope after your loss, you should first speak to your GP. They want to hear from you, and will be able to help you get the support you need.
There are organisations across Scotland that provide support after baby loss. They can help with various things, including giving you someone to talk to or providing information about what happens next.
